# Templates everywhere

*Calepin* uses templates for nearly all text transformations and assembly operations. Every rendered element (a figure, a code block, a callout, a heading) passes through a template. The page wrapper that adds `<html>` or `\documentclass` is a template. The navbar, sidebar, and footer of a website are templates. If you can see it in the output, there is a template behind it.

This means customization is always the same operation: find the template, edit it. No need to learn Rust or Go or Lua. Just write plain text!

It also means that *Calepin* projects are super LLM-friendly. Just ask your agent what you need, and it will almost certainly get it right:

> Go to the `index_calepin/templates` folder. Switch all the colors to a Studio Ghibli inspired pastel theme. Make the top navigation bar twice as wide. Align the footer text to the right.

{% include "assets/source_tip.html" %}

# Jinja2

Templates use [Jinja2](https://jinja.palletsprojects.com/) syntax (via [MiniJinja](https://github.com/mitsuhiko/minijinja), a Rust implementation). Jinja2 is one of the most popular templating systems in the world. It is easy to learn, powerful, and well-documented.

The core idea: write normal text, and mark locations where values should be inserted with double curly braces:

```
Hello, {{ name }}!
```

When the template is rendered with `name = "World"`, the output is `Hello, World!`. That is the basic mechanism. Everything else builds on it.

For a thorough introduction, see the [Jinja2 Template Designer Documentation](https://jinja.palletsprojects.com/en/3.1.x/templates/).


# Templates

Each template file controls one piece of output. They live in `{stem}_calepin/templates/`, organized by format:

```
{stem}_calepin/templates/
  html/         # HTML templates (figure.html, callout.html, main.html, ...)
  latex/        # LaTeX templates (figure.tex, main.tex, ...)
  typst/        # Typst templates (figure.typ, main.typ, ...)
  website/      # Website layout templates (navbar.html, sidebar.html, ...)
  common/       # Format-agnostic templates (.jinja)
```

Resolution is layered per file: *Calepin* checks sidecar templates, then project templates (`{stem}_calepin/templates/`), then extension templates, then built-in defaults. You only need to override the specific files you want to change; everything else falls through to the built-in templates.


# Element templates

Element templates control small, self-contained components. Here is the built-in emphasis template for HTML:

`html/emphasis.html`:

```html
<em>{{ text }}</em>
```

And for LaTeX:

`latex/emphasis.tex`:

```latex
\emph{ {{- text -}} }
```

That is the entire file. One line, one element. Every emphasis in the output passes through this template.


# Div templates

Fenced divs (`::: {.classname} ... :::`) use templates for larger structures like figures, callouts, theorems, and code blocks. These templates receive richer variables.

Here is the built-in figure template for Typst:

`typst/figure.typ`:

```
{%- set loc = cap_location | default("bottom") %}
#figure(
  image("{{src}}", width: {{width_attr | default("70%")}})
{%- if caption %}, caption: [{{caption}}]{%- endif %}
){% if label %} <{{label}}>{% endif %}
```

The template receives variables like `src`, `caption`, `label`, `width_attr`, and `cap_location`, which are set by *Calepin* based on the figure's attributes.


# Page assembly

The page template wraps the entire rendered body in a complete document. Here is a simplified version of the built-in LaTeX page template:

`latex/main.tex`:

```latex
\documentclass[11pt]{article}
\usepackage[T1]{fontenc}
\usepackage{graphicx,hyperref}
{{clp.bib_preamble}}
{{clp.preamble}}

{% if cfg.title %}\title{ {{-cfg.title-}} }{% endif %}
{% if clp.authors %}\author{ {{-clp.authors-}} }{% endif %}

\begin{document}
{% if cfg.title %}\maketitle{% endif %}

{{cfg.abstract}}
{{clp.toc}}
{{clp.body}}
{{clp.appendix}}
{{clp.bibliography}}
{{clp.bib_end}}
\end{document}
```

Variables are namespaced: `clp.*` for engine-computed values (`clp.body`, `clp.toc`, `clp.preamble`, `clp.bibliography`) and `cfg.*` for user-authored values (`cfg.title`, `cfg.abstract`). Custom front matter fields are also available: a field `custom_footer = "Confidential"` in your document becomes `{{cfg.custom_footer}}` in the page template.


# More powerful features

Jinja2 goes far beyond simple variable insertion. Here are three features that are especially useful in templates.

Conditionals let you vary output by format or by the presence of a variable:

```
{% if caption %}
<figcaption>{{caption}}</figcaption>
{% endif %}
```

Loops iterate over lists:

```
{% for item in keywords %}
\keyword{ {{- item -}} }
{% endfor %}
```

Filters transform values inline. Jinja2 provides `upper`, `lower`, `trim`, `replace`, `default`, `length`, and many others:

```
{{ title | upper }}
{{ width | default("100%") }}
```

Again, see the [Jinja2 documentation](https://jinja.palletsprojects.com/en/3.1.x/templates/) for the full syntax.


# Template management

*Calepin* provides several commands to inspect, override, and validate templates.

## Ejecting a single template

Instead of overriding all templates at once, you can eject just the one you need:

```bash
calepin templates eject figure doc.qmd
calepin templates eject main doc.qmd -t latex
```

This copies the built-in template into your sidecar so you can edit it. The rest of your templates continue to use built-in defaults. Use `--force` to overwrite an existing sidecar copy.

## Extending built-in templates

When you only want to change a small part of a template, copying the entire file means your override may become stale after a *Calepin* upgrade. Template inheritance solves this.

Use `{% extends "builtin:filename" %}` in your sidecar template to inherit from the built-in version and override only specific blocks:

```html
{% extends "builtin:figure.html" %}

{% block caption %}
<figcaption class="custom-caption">{{ cfg.caption }}</figcaption>
{% endblock %}
```

The `builtin:` prefix tells the template engine to load the original built-in template, regardless of any sidecar overrides. Your template inherits all blocks from the built-in and you only redefine the ones you need.

This works for both element templates (figure, div, code_source, etc.) and page templates (main, base). For this to work, the built-in template must define `{% block %}` regions. Check the built-in source with `calepin templates show` to see available blocks.

## Checking for outdated templates

After upgrading *Calepin*, your sidecar templates may no longer match the new built-in defaults:

```bash
calepin templates outdated doc.qmd
```

This lists every sidecar template that differs from its current built-in version. Use `calepin templates diff` to inspect the differences and `calepin templates reset <name>` to revert individual files.

## Inspecting template variables

To see which variables are available in a given template:

```bash
calepin templates vars figure doc.qmd
calepin templates vars main doc.qmd
```

Variables are namespaced: `cfg.*` for user-authored values (front matter, attributes), `clp.*` for engine-computed values (rendered content, format, assets), and `tpl.*` for template variant selections.

## Previewing a template

Test a template in isolation with sample data:

```bash
calepin templates preview figure doc.qmd
calepin templates preview code_source doc.qmd
```

This renders the template with representative sample variables and prints the output, useful for rapid iteration on template changes.

## Linting templates

Validate your sidecar templates for common issues:

```bash
calepin templates lint doc.qmd
calepin templates lint doc.qmd code_source
```

The linter checks for parse errors, unknown variable namespaces, deprecated patterns, mismatched block tags, and HTML in non-HTML templates.

## Debugging template provenance

When building, pass `--debug-templates` to annotate the HTML output with comments showing which template produced each element and whether it came from the sidecar or from built-in:

```bash
calepin render doc.qmd --debug-templates
```

The output will contain comments like:

```html
<!-- template:figure (sidecar) -->
<figure id="fig-example">...</figure>
<!-- /template:figure -->
```
